title: Quantifying the effect of canopy space competition on crown architecture using the terrestrial Light Detection and Ranging technology—a review
content:
Abstract
Tree crowns mediate light capture and therefore sit at the core of aboveground competition, yet crown-competition relationships have long been inferred from stem-centric proxies because repeated, three-dimensional (3D) crown measurements were historically impractical. Terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) has changed this by enabling rapid, non-destructive, high-density 3D mapping of crown geometry and internal structure, making it feasible to quantify competition as a spatial process occurring in canopy space rather than as an indirect outcome of neighbor size and distance. This review synthesizes how TLS has been used to characterize crown architecture and quantify canopy space competition, and how these data can refine theories of crown interactions and space filling, including departures from idealized symmetry assumptions. Using a structured Web of Science search spanning 2005–2025, the review identified 26 studies published between 2011–2025 that directly address TLS-based crown architecture and canopy space competition. We summarize the prevailing TLS-derived crown extraction workflow, illustrate canopy-level organization, how TLS enables crown-mediated competitor definition and indices, and direct quantification of mechanistic crown responses via crown plasticity. Across the literature, a consistent limitation is temporal sparseness, as most studies remain single-snapshot or two time-point designs, constraining inference on trajectories, rates, and sequencing of crown reorganization. We conclude by outlining priority directions for trajectory-based, neighborhood-aware, multitemporal TLS analyses that link evolving canopy interactions to growth, and competition modeling.
